case_analysis.focal_point: Whether state National Guard entities (and their adjutants general) function as a covered “federal agency” employer under the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute when supervising federally employed dual-status technicians, and whether applying the statute in that context is constitutional under the Militia Clauses.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute (FSLMRS), 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135; National Guard Technicians Act of 1968, codified as amended at 32 U.S.C. § 709 and related provisions defining technicians as federal employees (e.g., 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1)); U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16 (Militia Clauses).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Ohio Adjutant General’s Department and related state Guard entities), supported by several state amici, argue that a state National Guard and its adjutant general are not a “federal agency” for FSLMRS purposes and therefore cannot be subjected to FLRA jurisdiction based on their supervision of dual-status technicians. They contend the Technicians Act deliberately created a hybrid structure—technicians are federally paid civilian employees but are administered through state adjutants general as state military officials—so treating the Guard as a federal agency collapses that line and intrudes into state control of the militia. They also assert that applying federal collective-bargaining requirements in this setting conflicts with the Technicians Act’s command structure and, in their constitutional argument, impermissibly interferes with state authority reserved by the Militia Clauses (training, discipline, appointment of officers, and day-to-day military readiness functions). Some amici further warn of broader downstream consequences if state officials are recharacterized as federal agencies, and raise concerns that compelled union-related arrangements could trigger First Amendment problems.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (FLRA, supported by the federal government and the union intervenor) argue that dual-status technicians are expressly federal civilian employees and that, when adjutants general supervise them in their technician roles, they act as the relevant federal-employer representative for those federal employment conditions. On that view, the FSLMRS can apply without converting the state Guard into a general-purpose federal agency: it simply regulates labor-management relations for a category of federal civilian employment that Congress created and funds. Respondents maintain that the collective-bargaining regime is limited (i.e., subject to statutory exclusions for military matters and management rights) and is consistent with the Technicians Act’s structure, which contemplates federal employment protections alongside state administration. They also argue there is no Militia Clauses violation because Congress has broad authority over federal employment and over the Guard when operating within federally defined roles, and because bargaining is confined to conditions of federal civilian employment rather than core militia command prerogatives.
key_precedents: Ohio Adjutant General’s Department v. FLRA, 21 F.4th 401 (6th Cir. 2021)
Dyer v. Department of the Air Force, 971 F.3d 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2020)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point remains the definitional trigger in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3): FSLMRS applies to an “agency,” and a state adjutant general is not ordinarily an Executive agency—so we should be wary of silently reclassifying state officers. But Justice Kagan’s and Justice Thomas’s harmonization reading answers that textual objection on narrow grounds: 32 U.S.C. § 709(e) makes technicians employees of the Army or Air Force, and § 709(d) directs the Secretary to “designate” adjutants general to “employ and administer” those federal employees, which fits treating the adjutant general as the federal employer’s designated representative for that discrete civilian relationship rather than converting the Guard writ large into a federal agency. Perpich, as noted by Justices Alito and Thomas, reinforces that the Militia Clauses are grants of congressional power and do not supply a clear-statement rule that defeats Congress’s specific technician scheme, especially with FSLMRS’s management-rights and military carveouts doing limiting work. Under a minimalist approach, we can resolve the case by holding only that FSLMRS reaches technician bargaining insofar as the adjutant general acts in that federally designated employment capacity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: the FSLMRS turns on employment “in an agency” as defined in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), and a state adjutant general is not, in ordinary usage, an Executive agency. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Technicians Act supplies the necessary textual bridge by making technicians “employees of the Department of the Army or the Department of the Air Force,” 32 U.S.C. § 709(e), and directing the Secretary to “designate” adjutants general “to employ and administer” them, § 709(d), which is best read as assigning the adjutant general a limited federal employing-representative function rather than redefining the State Guard as a federal agency. Perpich, invoked by Roberts, cuts against importing a clear-statement/constitutional-avoidance overlay from the Militia Clauses because those clauses are grants of power to Congress, not a restraint that negates Congress’s express creation of a federal civilian employment relationship. Under an originalist and textualist approach, the harmonized reading—FSLMRS applies to the federal civilian employment slice Congress created—fits the enacted text better than the petitioner’s atextual carveout that would remove these federal employees from a generally applicable federal labor-relations scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s definitional point about “agency” in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3) is the best textual objection, but it loses force once we read the FSLMRS alongside the Technicians Act’s specific mechanics: technicians are federal employees of the Army or Air Force, and the Secretary “designate[s] the adjutants general … to employ and administer” them, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d), (e). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the narrow and textually coherent understanding is not that a State Guard becomes an Executive agency, but that the adjutant general acts as the federal employer’s designated representative for this discrete federal civilian employment relationship. Perpich, as Justice Thomas notes, treats the Militia Clauses as grants of congressional power in this domain, reducing the need for a clear-statement canon to avoid constitutional friction, especially given the FSLMRS’s management-rights and military exclusions that limit intrusion into core command and readiness. I therefore remain with the Respondent because petitioners’ reading would require an implausible statutory discontinuity—federal employees created and funded by Congress, yet categorically outside the baseline federal labor-relations scheme—without Congress clearly saying so.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point remains the definitional trigger: the FSLMRS speaks in terms of an “agency” under 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), and a state adjutant general is not ordinarily an Executive agency. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Technicians Act’s specific mechanism—technicians are federal civilian employees, and the Secretary “designate[s] the adjutants general … to employ and administer” them, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d), (e)—is best read as placing the adjutant general in a limited federal representative capacity for this discrete employment relationship, harmonizing the statutes without recharacterizing the Guard writ large. Perpich, as Justice Thomas notes, undercuts the claim that the Militia Clauses require a clear-statement rule here; coupled with the FSLMRS’s management-rights and military exclusions, the practical intrusion into command/readiness is meaningfully cabined. On my pragmatic view, Gorsuch’s reading would unnecessarily strip a vulnerable class of federal employees of Congress’s baseline labor framework despite Congress having structured their employment as federal in key respects.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s definitional point about “agency” in § 7103(a)(3) is the hardest textual obstacle, but it doesn’t defeat the narrower reading that the FSLMRS regulates the federal employment relationship Congress created for dual-status technicians rather than reclassifying the State Guard as an Executive agency. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d)’s directive that the Secretary “designate” the adjutants general “to employ and administer” technicians, combined with § 709(e)’s statement that technicians are employees of the Army or Air Force, supports treating the adjutant general as the federal employer’s designated representative for that limited function—enough to make the bargaining duties operate on the federal side of the hybrid arrangement. Perpich, as Roberts and Justice Thomas note, reinforces that the Militia Clauses are affirmative grants of authority and thus do not supply a clear-statement rule that would override Congress’s express technician-employment structure, especially given the FSLMRS’s management-rights and military exclusions that keep core command/readiness matters off the bargaining table. Johnson v. Orr (noted by Justice Sotomayor) doesn’t do the statutory work by itself, but it corroborates that our role-specific “representative capacity” reading matches how the scheme has long functioned and avoids the atextual consequence of stripping federal employees of the federal labor framework without Congress saying so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s harmonization move—that § 709(d) makes the adjutant general the Secretary’s “representative” for FSLMRS purposes—does real work, but it does so by implication where Congress elsewhere supplied an express definitional trigger. The FSLMRS applies only when employees are “in an agency” as defined in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), and neither § 709(d)’s “designate … to employ and administer” nor § 709(e)’s “employees of the Department” text deems a state adjutant general an “Executive agency” or a Title 5 “representative of an agency” for collective bargaining; that’s a separate, affirmative statutory step Congress knows how to take. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Johnson v. Orr may show that adjutants general act as federal agents in some contexts, but lower-court gloss cannot amend the statutory definition or supply the clear statement needed to subject state officers to a federal labor-relations regime with attendant separation-of-powers and federalism friction. Perpich confirms Guard hybridity and Congress’s power, but it does not answer the antecedent textual question whether Congress actually extended the FSLMRS’s bargaining obligations to these state officials rather than to the federal Departments directly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch is right to press the definitional point that the FSLMRS turns on an "agency" in § 7103(a)(3), and a state adjutant general is not naturally an Executive agency; but Chief Justice Roberts’s harmonization reading answers that objection by treating the adjutant general as the Secretary’s designated employing representative only for the discrete federal-civilian technician relationship Congress created in 32 U.S.C. § 709(d), (e). Perpich, as Roberts and Justice Thomas note, cuts against importing a freestanding clear-statement rule from the Guard’s hybrid character because the Militia Clauses are affirmative grants to Congress, and here Congress expressly federalized technician employment while cabining intrusion via the FSLMRS management-rights and military exclusions. I also find Justice Kagan’s emphasis on § 709(f)’s federally controlled separation consequences persuasive evidence that Congress expected federal employment rules to attach in this slice of the program, making it unlikely Congress silently stripped these federal employees of the Statute’s baseline protections. On my institutionalist and precedent-respecting approach, the longstanding workable administrative practice and the narrower representative-capacity construction avoid unnecessary constitutional friction without rewriting § 7103’s definition.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point remains the definitional trigger in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3): a State Guard and a state adjutant general are not, in the ordinary sense, an “Executive agency,” and we should not lightly treat state officials as federal agencies without textual warrant. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan identify the critical textual bridge: 32 U.S.C. § 709(e) makes technicians employees of the Department of the Army or Air Force, and § 709(d) requires the Secretary to “designate” adjutants general “to employ and administer” those federal employees—best read as a narrow, role-specific delegation that makes the adjutant general the federal employer’s representative for technician civilian employment rather than converting the Guard wholesale into an “agency.” Perpich, as Justice Thomas notes, frames the Militia Clauses as grants of power to Congress and thus does not supply a clear-statement overlay that would negate Congress’s express federal-employee designation and administration mechanism. Johnson v. Orr (raised by Justice Sotomayor) is not dispositive, but it is consistent with this reading in recognizing that adjutants general can act in a federal capacity in this statutory scheme, reinforcing rather than undermining the harmonized textual account.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point remains the Title 5 definitional chain: the FSLMRS attaches to an “agency,” and a state adjutant general is not ordinarily one under § 7103(a)(3). But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Technicians Act expressly makes dual-status technicians federal employees of the Army/Air Force and then directs the Secretary to “designate” adjutants general to “employ and administer” them, which is naturally read as a limited federal-representative capacity rather than a wholesale reclassification of the State Guard. Perpich, noted by Roberts and Thomas, undercuts the constitutional-avoidance/clear-statement pressure by confirming the Militia Clauses are affirmative grants permitting Congress to structure this hybrid program, and the FSLMRS’s management-rights and military exclusions mitigate practical intrusion into command/readiness. Pragmatically, Gorsuch’s no-coverage reading would strip a defined set of federal civilian employees of Congress’s labor-relations regime without a clearer textual directive to that effect, and I don’t see his definitional objection as strong enough to override the harmonizing reading of §§ 709(d), (e), and (f).

John Roberts.reasoning: Dual-status technicians are expressly designated federal civilian employees, see 32 U.S.C. § 709 and 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1), and Congress designed their employment conditions to be governed by federal law even though day-to-day supervision is carried out through state adjutants general. Reading the FSLMRS to cover the adjutant general in that limited, representative capacity when setting technicians’ civilian conditions of employment is the narrow construction that best harmonizes the Statute with the Technicians Act and preserves institutional stability. Petitioners’ Militia Clauses objection fails because the Clauses are grants of authority to Congress rather than a constraint, and applying collective-bargaining rules to federal civilian employment does not regulate the State’s appointment, training, or command of the militia in its military capacity. Cf. Perpich v. Dep’t of Def., 496 U.S. 334, 349 (1990).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Technicians Act makes dual-status technicians federal civilian employees, see 32 U.S.C. § 709 (and related provisions identifying them as federal employees), so applying the FSLMRS to their civilian employment is consistent with the statute’s text and does not require recharacterizing the State Guard itself as a general-purpose federal agency. When an adjutant general supervises technicians in their technician capacity, he functions as the federal employer’s representative for those federal employment conditions, and the FSLMRS’s limits on bargaining (e.g., management rights and exclusions for military matters) reduce any claimed intrusion into militia command. Under the Militia Clauses, Congress possesses affirmative authority to organize and govern the militia when operating within federally defined roles, and those Clauses do not operate as freestanding limits on Congress’s power to regulate federal employment. Perpich confirms the Militia Clauses are grants of authority to Congress rather than constraints, and thus there is no constitutional barrier to regulating technicians’ civilian employment on the same terms as other federal employees.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of the Technicians Act makes dual-status technicians “employees of the Department of the Army or the Department of the Air Force” (32 U.S.C. § 709(e)) and thus federal civilian employees, so when an adjutant general administers their technician employment, he is functioning as the federal-employer representative for that federal job rather than as a purely state employer under the FSLMRS. The FSLMRS’s collective-bargaining obligations can operate here without reclassifying the state Guard as a general federal agency because the regime is confined to conditions of federal civilian employment and is constrained by statutory exclusions and management rights (5 U.S.C. §§ 7103, 7106). Petitioners’ Militia Clauses argument overreads those provisions: the Militia Clauses are affirmative grants of authority to Congress, not freestanding limits, and Perpich confirms Congress’s broad power to structure and regulate the Guard as part of building an effective national force (496 U.S. 334, 349 (1990)). Given that limited application, applying the FSLMRS to technician employment does not unconstitutionally intrude on core state militia prerogatives such as appointment of officers or military command and discipline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Dual-status technicians are expressly federal civilian employees under the Technicians Act, 32 U.S.C. § 709, and related federal definitions (e.g., 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1)), so when an adjutant general supervises their technician duties he functions as the federal employer’s representative for purposes of the FSLMRS, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135. Applying the FSLMRS here does not unconstitutionally intrude on state militia prerogatives because it regulates conditions of federal civilian employment, while the statute and the labor regime preserve exclusions for military matters and management rights, avoiding interference with core command and readiness functions. Petitioners’ Militia Clauses theory misreads those Clauses as constraints rather than affirmative grants of congressional authority, and Congress may attach federal employment rules to a federally created and funded workforce that supports Guard readiness. Perpich confirms the Guard’s federal–state character and that the Militia Clauses empower Congress in this domain, supporting constitutionality of regulating technicians’ civilian status without converting the entire state Guard into a general-purpose federal agency.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSLMRS covers employees “employed in an agency,” and while a State National Guard is not itself an “Executive agency” under 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), Congress in the Technicians Act expressly makes dual-status technicians federal civilian employees and directs that the Secretary “designate[s] the adjutants general … to employ and administer” them, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d), with federally mandated consequences for separation, § 709(f)(1). In that discrete technician-employer capacity, the adjutant general functions as the federal government’s designated employing representative, consistent with decisions recognizing that adjutants general act as federal agents when administering the technician program (e.g., Johnson v. Orr, 780 F.2d 386, 392 (3d Cir. 1986)). Applied this way, the FSLMRS regulates conditions of federal civilian employment (subject to management-rights and military exclusions) and does not commandeer state militia command, so it is workable and coherent with the statutory scheme and does not violate the Militia Clauses.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSLMRS applies only to an “agency,” defined in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3) by reference to “Executive agency” in Title 5—terms that, in ordinary public meaning and statutory usage, do not encompass a State National Guard or a state adjutant general acting as a state officer, even when administering federally funded dual-status technicians under 32 U.S.C. § 709. Nothing in § 709(d) or (e) converts the adjutant general into the Department of the Army or Air Force; at most, those provisions require compliance with federal regulations while preserving a state-administered command structure. Reading the statute to treat state officials as federal “agency” employers would stretch the text and raise serious separation-of-powers and Militia Clauses concerns by subjecting state militia administration to federal labor-relations control absent a clear statement. Perpich v. Department of Defense confirms the Guard’s dual state/federal character, and that very hybridity counsels against reclassifying state Guard components as federal agencies without unmistakable congressional direction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Dual-status technicians are expressly federal civilian employees under the Technicians Act, 32 U.S.C. § 709, and 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1), and the FSLMRS applies by its terms to labor-management relations for federal employees, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135. Treating the adjutant general as the “representative of an agency” for purposes of bargaining over technicians’ civilian conditions of employment does not convert the State Guard into a general federal agency; it implements Congress’s chosen federal employment framework while leaving military command and readiness matters protected by statutory exclusions and management rights in the FSLMRS. Under Perpich v. Department of Defense (1990), Congress has substantial authority under the Militia Clauses and related powers to structure and regulate National Guard personnel when operating within federally defined roles, and applying a federal labor statute to federal civilian employment administered through state officials does not unconstitutionally displace the States’ reserved militia prerogatives. Respect for longstanding administrative practice and workability also counsels against a destabilizing reclassification that would strip technicians of uniform federal labor protections despite their federal employment status.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSLMRS defines “agency” to include an “Executive agency,” 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), and Congress has expressly made dual-status technicians federal civilian employees, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d); 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1), so the statute’s ordinary meaning supports treating the adjutant general as the federal employer’s representative when setting conditions of that federal civilian employment. That application does not convert the State Guard wholesale into a federal agency; it regulates labor-management relations only for a federal position Congress created and funds, subject to statutory limits that exclude military matters and preserve management rights, see 5 U.S.C. §§ 7106, 7117. Nor does this arrangement violate the Militia Clauses, because those Clauses are grants of authority to Congress and do not bar Congress from regulating federally defined roles tied to federal employment, consistent with Perpich v. Department of Defense, 496 U.S. 334, 349 (1990). To the extent there is any tension with the Technicians Act’s hybrid administration, the more specific technician provisions still leave technicians as federal employees whose civilian employment conditions may be governed by generally applicable federal labor statutes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Dual-status technicians are expressly designated federal civilian employees, see 32 U.S.C. § 709 and 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1), so Congress may subject their civilian employment conditions to the FSLMRS, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135, even when day-to-day supervision is carried out by a state adjutant general acting in that federal-employer capacity. Interpreting the adjutant general as the relevant “agency” representative for technician employment effectuates the Statute’s purpose while preserving the Technicians Act’s military/civilian divide, because bargaining remains limited by statutory exclusions and management rights that protect core command and readiness functions. Petitioners’ Militia Clauses objection overreads those provisions: they are affirmative grants of authority to Congress, not freestanding limitations, and Perpich v. Department of Defense confirms Congress’s broad power to structure and regulate the Guard’s federally defined roles. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences, denying FLRA coverage would strip a category of federal employees of the labor-relations framework Congress enacted without a clear statutory command to do so.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether state National Guard adjutants general and their Guard units can be treated as a federal “agency”/“employer” subject to the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute when supervising federally appointed and paid dual-status technicians, and whether applying that statute in this context is consistent with the Militia Clauses and the National Guard Technicians Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute (FSLMRS), 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135; National Guard Technicians Act of 1968, codified at 32 U.S.C. § 709; dual-status technician definition at 10 U.S.C. § 10216; U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16 (Militia Clauses).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Ohio Adjutant General’s Department and related state-Guard entities) argue that state National Guards and state adjutants general are state institutions, not federal “agencies,” so the FLRA lacks authority to regulate their labor relations as if they were a federal employer; they contend the Technicians Act’s structure places technicians in a hybrid status but preserves state control through the adjutant general, and that forcing bargaining/FLRA oversight over technician-related management decisions intrudes on state sovereign prerogatives and conflicts with the Militia Clauses’ allocation of authority over the militia (training/discipline and appointment of officers) and with Congress’s specific technician scheme.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (FLRA, supported by the federal government and the union) argue that dual-status technicians are federal civilian employees appointed under federal law and paid with federal funds, and that when an adjutant general supervises technicians’ civilian employment he functions as part of the federal labor-management regime Congress created; thus the FSLMRS permissibly applies to technician working conditions (with statutory limits protecting military matters), does not convert the Guard into a general-purpose federal agency, and does not violate the Militia Clauses because the bargaining duty concerns federal civilian employment conditions rather than core militia command, training, discipline, or officer appointment reserved to the states.
key_precedents: Dyer v. Department of the Air Force, 971 F.3d 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2020)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the textual and clear-statement concern (Hancock v. Train): “agency” in § 7103 does not naturally encompass a State Guard or adjutant general, and we should not lightly presume Congress subjected core state militia functions to FLRA control. But that objection is answered by a narrow, statute-specific reading: as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress itself created a federal civilian employment relationship for dual-status technicians in 32 U.S.C. § 709 and expressly designated the adjutant general to “employ and administer” those federal positions, so FLRA jurisdiction can attach only to that federally created employment slice without recharacterizing the Guard generally as a federal agency. Perpich reinforces that Congress may attach federal incidents to the Guard’s federalized aspects, and by confining bargaining to civilian “conditions of employment” (excluding military command, training, discipline, and officer appointment), we avoid unnecessary constitutional friction and preserve institutional legitimacy. On my minimalist approach, the best course is a limited holding that harmonizes the two statutes and leaves broader state-sovereignty questions for a case that squarely presents them.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s “limited-slice” approach is the strongest counterargument, but it still asks us to treat a state adjutant general as a federal “agency” without statutory text doing that work. Section 709’s delegation to “the adjutant general of the jurisdiction concerned” (and related provisions about federal pay/benefits) may federalize the technician’s status, but it does not amend 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3)’s definition of “agency” or supply the clear statement Hancock v. Train requires before we presume Congress subjected state militia command structures—administered by state officers—to an additional federal labor-relations regime. As Justice Alito notes, any purported civilian-only bargaining boundary is not a textual limitation in the FSLMRS’s “agency” trigger and predictably collapses into supervision, discipline, and readiness questions that Congress would have confronted explicitly if it meant FLRA jurisdiction to attach. Perpich confirms Congress has significant power over the Guard, but it cannot substitute for the missing words in the labor statute, so the respondents’ function-based harmonization does not overcome the text-based jurisdictional defect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I understand Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “slice-specific” construction, echoed by Justices Kagan and Barrett, but it still relies on recharacterizing a state adjutant general as a federal “agency” for some purposes without any clear textual hook in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3). Section 709’s directive that the adjutant general “employ and administer” technicians establishes a federal employment relationship, as Justice Sotomayor stresses, yet it does not follow that Congress also subjected that state military chain of command to FLRA supervision—Hancock’s clear-statement principle is triggered precisely because the administrative decisions at issue predictably implicate readiness, supervision, and discipline even if labeled “civilian conditions.” Perpich, invoked by Justices Gorsuch and Kagan, confirms Congress’s power over the Guard’s federal aspects, but it cannot supply missing statutory text or overcome the deliberate choice in § 709 to lodge authority in “the adjutant general of the jurisdiction concerned,” which cuts against importing an additional federal labor-relations overlay by implication. Because the respondents’ limiting principle depends on functional line-drawing rather than the enacted definition of “agency,” I would hold the FLRA lacks jurisdiction absent a clearer statement from Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s clear-statement argument rightly forces us to identify the textual hook, but § 709 provides it by expressly creating a federal civilian employment relationship and delegating to the adjutant general the authority to “employ and administer” those federal positions—so applying the FSLMRS in that narrow lane is not an implied regulation of the State’s militia writ large. Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction is the practical and legally disciplined answer: FLRA coverage can be confined to technicians’ civilian “conditions of employment,” leaving command, discipline, training, and officer appointment outside bargaining and avoiding the Militia Clauses concerns. Hancock’s caution about intruding on state sovereignty has less bite where Congress has already federalized the job and is simply specifying the administering official, rather than commandeering a state program. Given the real-world stakes for a workforce Congress treated as federal employees, I see no genuine statutory or constitutional incompatibility that warrants stripping them of the labor protections Congress provided.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best pushback: § 7103’s definition of “agency” is framed in federal-institutional terms, and Hancock’s clear-statement instinct cautions against reading a state adjutant general into that category by implication. But Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction answers the textual concern without functional freewheeling: Congress in § 709 expressly creates federally funded civilian positions and assigns the adjutant general to “employ and administer” them, so for that statutorily delimited slice the adjutant general is the designated employing instrumentality of a federal employment relationship rather than a general-purpose state “agency.” On that reading, FLRA authority is confined to civilian “conditions of employment” and does not reach militia command, training, discipline, or officer appointment—so the Hancock concern is materially weaker because Congress is not regulating the State’s sovereign operations, but attaching federal labor-relations incidents to a federal job it created. Justice Jackson’s emphasis that this avoids a broader reclassification of the Guard while preserving coherence between the Technicians Act and the labor statute reinforces that the narrower textual harmonization is the best reading.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly press that “agency” in § 7103 ordinarily denotes a federal entity and that Hancock’s clear-statement instinct counsels caution before treating a state adjutant general as one. But the Technicians Act supplies the needed textual hook: Congress itself creates a federal civilian employment relationship and then specifies that the adjutant general shall “employ and administer” those federal positions under federal rules, 32 U.S.C. § 709(d), so the adjutant general is the statutorily designated administering authority for that federal employment slice, not a free-standing state institution beyond federal reach. Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction answers the bleed-over concern by confining bargaining/FLRA oversight to civilian “conditions of employment” and excluding military command, training, discipline, and officer appointment; on that reading, Hancock’s concern about regulating core state functions is substantially diminished because Congress is attaching federal incidents to a federally created job rather than commandeering the State’s militia prerogatives. Nothing in Perpich supplies missing statutory text, but it does confirm Congress may attach such federal conditions to Guard-related employment without collapsing the Guard’s dual character.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the most serious point: “agency” in § 7103 is not naturally read to include a state adjutant general, and Hancock’s clear-statement instinct is a legitimate constraint when federal law intrudes on core state institutions. But Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction answers that objection in a way consistent with my institutional, precedent-respecting approach: we are not deeming the Guard a federal agency writ large; we are recognizing that Congress created a federal civilian employment relationship in § 709 and designated the adjutant general as the administering federal employing authority for that narrow slice. Perpich reinforces that Congress may attach federal incidents to the Guard when operating in its federally structured capacity, and confining bargaining to civilian “conditions of employment” avoids bleed-over into militia command, training, discipline, or officer appointment. Given the long-settled practice sustaining FLRA jurisdiction in this lane and the availability of this narrow, constitutionally avoidant reading, I do not see Thomas/Alito’s textual objection as sufficient to justify a disruptive carveout absent a clearer conflict in the statutory scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best textual point that “agency” in § 7103(a)(3) ordinarily denotes a federal executive entity and that Hancock-like clear-statement concerns caution against reading state military institutions into a federal labor statute by implication. But Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction answers that objection on the statutes’ own terms: Congress expressly made dual-status technicians federal civilian employees and, in § 709(d), specified the adjutant general as the official who “employ[s] and administer[s]” that federally created employment relationship, which supplies the necessary clarity for this narrow slice without reclassifying the Guard as a federal agency writ large. Perpich—cited by several colleagues—reinforces that Congress may attach federal incidents to the Guard’s federally defined roles, and the avoidance-minded cabining to civilian “conditions of employment” (excluding military command, discipline, training, and officer-appointment matters) prevents the bleed-over Justice Alito fears and keeps the holding within the original public meaning of the Technician scheme’s delegation. Under my textualist methodology, the specific federal-employment provisions in § 709 and § 10216 can operate as the clear statement that the FSLMRS’s labor-relations rules apply to that federal employment, even if “agency” would not ordinarily reach a State adjutant general outside this federally assigned function.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press that § 7103’s definition of “agency” does not, on its face, name a state adjutant general, and Hancock’s clear-statement impulse is not trivial when federal regulation touches a state military apparatus. But that argument loses force once we take § 709 seriously as the “clear statement” Congress did make: it federalizes the technician employment relationship (appointment, pay, benefits, removal) and then affirmatively delegates to the adjutant general the authority to “employ and administer” those federal civilian positions, which is enough to treat him as the employing instrumentality for that slice without recharacterizing the Guard writ large. Chief Justice Roberts’s limiting construction—FLRA jurisdiction confined to civilian “conditions of employment,” excluding core command, training, discipline, and officer appointment—answers the spillover concern Justice Alito raises and fits a pragmatic, avoidance-minded approach that preserves both statutory schemes. Perpich, as several colleagues note, reinforces that Congress can attach federal incidents to the Guard’s federally integrated functions; it doesn’t supply missing text, but it confirms the constitutional headroom for the narrow statutory reading we adopt here.

John Roberts.reasoning: The National Guard Technicians Act, 32 U.S.C. § 709, makes dual-status technicians federal civilian employees for their technician duties (appointed and paid under federal law), and the FSLMRS, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135, can be applied on narrow grounds to that civilian employment relationship without recharacterizing the State Guard as a general-purpose federal “agency.” Maryland for Use of Levin v. United States, 381 U.S. 41 (1965), recognizes the Guard’s dual federal/state character, supporting Congress’s authority to attach federal incidents to Guard functions when acting within its enumerated powers; here, bargaining obligations may be confined to civilian working conditions and not core militia command, training, discipline, or officer appointment reserved to the States under Art. I, § 8, cl. 16. Reading the statutes to permit FLRA oversight only to the extent it regulates the federal employment of technicians avoids unnecessary constitutional confrontation and preserves institutional legitimacy through a limited, precedent-respecting resolution. Because Congress has created a federal employment structure for technicians and can condition that structure with federal labor-relations rules, the FLRA may treat the adjutant general as the relevant federal “employer” when supervising technicians’ civilian work under § 709.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSLMRS applies to a federal “agency”/“employer,” 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135, and the ordinary meaning of those terms does not encompass a State’s National Guard or its adjutant general acting pursuant to state authority; reading the Statute to treat state-Guard entities as federal agencies stretches the text beyond what Congress enacted. The National Guard Technicians Act, 32 U.S.C. § 709, deliberately vests technician hiring, supervision, and discipline in “the adjutant general of the jurisdiction concerned,” preserving state control over the Guard’s internal administration even while technicians are federally funded—a specific scheme that should not be displaced by a more general federal labor statute absent a clear statement. Applying the FSLMRS here also risks intrusion into the States’ constitutional prerogatives under the Militia Clauses, U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16, which reserve to the States the appointment of officers and authority to train the militia according to federally prescribed discipline; Perpich v. Dep’t of Def., 496 U.S. 334 (1990), recognizes broad congressional power but does not authorize converting state militia structures into federal agencies for domestic labor regulation without clear textual warrant. Given the hybrid status of dual-status technicians (10 U.S.C. § 10216; 32 U.S.C. § 709), the better reading is that Congress regulated them through the Technicians Act while keeping their day-to-day Guard supervision in state hands, beyond FLRA jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSLMRS applies to a federal “agency,” 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(3), and Congress did not make an unmistakably clear statement that state National Guard units or state adjutants general are to be treated as a federal agency/employer merely because they supervise federally funded dual-status technicians under 32 U.S.C. § 709. Under the clear-statement principle reflected in Hancock v. Train, 426 U.S. 167 (1976), we should not presume Congress meant to subject core state military institutions to federal labor-relations regulation absent explicit text, particularly where the Militia Clauses reserve substantial state authority over militia organization and command (Art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16). The Technicians Act’s hybrid scheme—technicians as federal civilian employees but employed “by the adjutant general” under federal regulations, § 709(d), (e)—is better read as preserving state control of Guard administration while allowing federal funding/standards, not as converting the State’s Guard chain of command into a federal “agency.” Extending FLRA bargaining/ULP oversight into day-to-day Guard supervision risks practical interference with military readiness and discipline, consequences Congress would have addressed directly if intended.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Dual-status technicians are federally created, federally appointed, and federally paid civilian employees under the National Guard Technicians Act, 32 U.S.C. § 709, and 10 U.S.C. § 10216, so Congress may subject their civilian working conditions to the federal labor regime in the FSLMRS, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135. When an adjutant general supervises technicians in their technician capacity, he is administering a federal employment scheme, and applying the FSLMRS in that limited sphere does not transform the Guard’s broader military functions into a federal “agency.” The Militia Clauses reserve to the States officer appointment and training authority, U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16, but bargaining over civilian terms and conditions of federal employment does not commandeer core militia command, discipline, or appointments—consistent with this Court’s recognition that technician work is civilian rather than militia service. That pragmatic reading preserves state prerogatives in military matters while protecting technicians’ access to fair labor processes Congress provided for federal employees.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Textually and structurally, the Technicians Act makes dual-status technicians federal civilian employees appointed under 32 U.S.C. § 709 and paid with federal funds, so when an adjutant general manages their civilian employment he is functioning as the statutorily designated federal employer for that slice of work. The FSLMRS applies to "agencies" in the federal labor system, and reading it to reach the technician-employment relationship best fits Congress’s coherent design: federal employment rules for the civilian job, while preserving military command through the Act’s and FSLMRS’s carveouts for military matters. That application is also consistent with the Militia Clauses because, as Perpich explains, those Clauses are affirmative grants of authority to Congress (not limitations), and regulating the terms and conditions of federal civilian employment does not usurp the States’ reserved control over militia appointment, training, and discipline. This is a workable, middle-ground interpretation that respects the Guard’s dual character without converting state Guards generally into federal agencies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Technicians Act makes dual-status technicians federal civilian employees appointed and paid under federal law, 32 U.S.C. § 709, and the FSLMRS applies by its terms to federal “agencies” employing such personnel, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7103(a)(3), (a)(2). While a state adjutant general is a state officer, in supervising technicians’ civilian employment he executes a federally created employment relationship and may be treated as the relevant “agency” employer for that limited purpose without transforming the Guard into a general federal instrumentality. The Militia Clauses are affirmative grants of authority to Congress, not freestanding limitations, and Congress may regulate federal civilian employment conditions connected to Guard readiness so long as it does not displace the States’ reserved powers over officer appointment and militia training/discipline, U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16; Perpich v. Dep’t of Def., 496 U.S. 334, 349 (1990). Given that the bargaining duty here concerns technicians’ civilian working conditions within Congress’s statutory scheme—and not core military command decisions—the application of the FSLMRS is consistent with § 709 and the Constitution.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the National Guard Technicians Act, dual-status technicians are federally created, federally appointed civilian employees paid with federal funds, 32 U.S.C. § 709 and 10 U.S.C. § 10216, and Congress has long subjected federal civilian employment to the FSLMRS’s collective-bargaining framework, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7101–7135. Applying the FSLMRS to an adjutant general’s supervision of technicians in their civilian capacity is consistent with the Guard’s hybrid structure recognized in Perpich v. Department of Defense (1990) and does not trench on the Militia Clauses’ reservations concerning officer appointment and militia training/discipline because the bargaining duty targets civilian working conditions, not core command functions. The statutory scheme is also practically workable and supported by entrenched lower-court practice sustaining FLRA jurisdiction in technician labor disputes, and judicial restraint counsels against upsetting that settled regime absent a clear constitutional conflict. Any remaining state-control interests are addressed by the Act’s built-in limits preserving military matters outside bargaining, avoiding a reading that would silently carve state Guards out of Congress’s comprehensive federal labor statute when they act as the employing entity for federal technicians.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSLMRS applies to a covered federal “agency” as “employer,” 5 U.S.C. §§ 7102, 7103(a)(3), (a)(4), and dual-status technicians are expressly federal civilian employees appointed and paid under federal law, 32 U.S.C. § 709; 10 U.S.C. § 10216. Textually, when an adjutant general supervises technicians’ civilian employment pursuant to § 709, he is administering a federal employment relationship Congress created, and applying the FSLMRS to bargaining over civilian “conditions of employment” fits that statutory design while leaving military command and discipline outside the bargaining obligation. Petitioners’ Militia Clauses argument is not supported by the Constitution’s text as construed in Perpich, which describes the Militia Clauses as affirmative grants of authority to Congress over the Guard’s federal aspects, 496 U.S. at 349, and the Technicians Act’s hybrid structure confirms Congress’s choice to regulate technicians as civilian employees while preserving specified state officer-appointment and militia prerogatives. Precedent and methodological consistency thus favor treating the relevant supervisory function as federal for purposes of the FSLMRS without reclassifying the Guard wholesale as a federal agency.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Congress expressly made dual-status technicians federal civilian employees appointed and paid under federal law, while directing that the service secretaries “designate[] the adjutants general … to employ and administer” them. 32 U.S.C. § 709(d); see also 10 U.S.C. § 10216(a)(1)(A). Given that federal delegation and the adjutant general’s federally prescribed authority to hire and to separate technicians from their technician employment, § 709(f), the adjutant general functions as the federal employer for those civilian positions, making application of the FSLMRS to technician working conditions consistent with the statutory scheme. This construction also avoids Militia Clause conflict because bargaining/FLRA oversight is limited to the technicians’ federal civilian employment conditions and does not displace state authority over militia officer appointment, training, or discipline under Art. I, § 8, cls. 15–16.
